title: The naive framing: "can Claude just answer my support tickets?"
text: Someone asked if Claude can just answer their support tickets fully on its own. Not quite, it drafts them. So, here's the real question. Can Claude just draft my support tickets? If you have

title: The queue arrives anytime
text: Customers, you have support and it doesn't wait. A queue that fills overnight, questions that don't clock out. Left alone, it eats your day in fragments. The support plugin turns that

title: Burden, or process
text: Burden into a process. For a solo operator, it's the difference between reacting all day and running a system that handles the queue for you. For a small team, it does something

title: Five voices, one
text: Else, one consistent voice. Instead of five people answering five different ways, every reply carries the same tone and the same facts. So, the natural read

title: So it just answers them? — the wrong guess
text: Is that it's fully automatic. It reads the ticket, writes the reply, and sends it. Support on autopilot, no human in the loop. Here's a case. A customer's

title: The customer who breaks that
text: Payment has failed three times. They've been with you two years and they're angry. Send that on autopilot and you risk getting the tone wrong on the one account that can't afford it. So, it doesn't send. It drafts and waits for you. Under the hood, it does four

title: Four jobs, one plugin
text: Concrete jobs. Triage the queue, draft the replies, build a knowledge base, and read sentiment. Not magic, four jobs it does well. Triage first. As requests

title: Sort the wall
text: Land, it sorts them. What needs you now, what can wait, and what's a known issue with a standard answer. The queue stops being a wall and becomes a sorted list. Then drafting. It generates replies that

title: Draft, on-brand
text: Fit the moment, pulling from your configured tone, your knowledge base, and the specific request in front of it. A first draft, not a form letter. Third, sentiment. Not every request is equal.

title: Find the ones who matter
text: It flags the frustrated and the at risk, the customer who needs a human now. It points your attention at the messages that actually need it. And it doesn't start from nothing. It reads your

title: Real conversations, not blank
text: Existing support inbox for context and mines the questions you've already answered to draft a structured FAQ. Your scattered experience becomes a help center. One setup step makes it yours.

title: Set the tone, set the tripwires
text: You set the tone, warm, efficient, or both, and escalation triggers, the words and situations that skip the standard answer and route straight to you. You decide what always reaches a human. In practice, handed the overnight queue and ask what's urgent, what's routine,

title: Thirty focused minutes
text: And what you can answer in a line. The payoff is time. A morning that might otherwise stretch into two fragmented hours compresses into 30 focused minutes. Back to that angry customer. Claude drafts in your tone, acknowledges the

title: The anchor returns: the plugin caught the tone
text: Frustration, explains the issue, proposes a fix. You read it, add a personal line only you would know to add, and send. The plugin caught the tone, you caught the context. And every FAQ entry pays forward. Claude finds the

title: Answer once, reuse forever
text: Questions you keep answering, ranks the top 10, and drafts each one. Publish it, and that's one question you never fielded again. Volume that quietly falls instead of climbing. For a live reply to an actual customer, the rule never relaxes. Draft, review,

title: Review, every time
text: Then send. That's where your judgment catches what the plugin can't see, the exception, the fragile account, the case autopilot would get wrong. But for the FAQ, the rule flips. You review an answer once, publish it, and it serves every future

title: Publish once, runs alone
text: Customer who asks that question without you touching it again. Same drafts, a different rule once they go public. Claude drafts every reply. You're still the one who decides what actually gets sent.

title: Carry-out
text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude. I run support for small business and want to set up the support plugin. First, ask me the five questions my customers ask

title: Your turn
text: Most, the tone my replies should carry, and the situations that must always reach me personally. Then draft FAQ answers for those five, a reusable reply template in my tone, and a short list of escalation triggers I should configure. Claude on call, the support plugin. Liam in for Bear.
